activities.anchor: the hot exhaust is the evidence
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the hot exhaust
activities.name: hvacExhaustPredict

config.q: Stand by an air conditioner's outdoor unit on a hot day and hot air pours out. What is the machine doing?
choices: Moving heat from indoors to outdoors
config.why: The trade's founding insight: heat is energy in transit, always moving from warmer to cooler — never the reverse unless a machine spends work to force it.

activities.anchor: Two more concepts carry the rest of the trade
activities.caption: fill the two kinds of heat
activities.name: hvacSensibleCloze

config.text: Sensible heat changes a substance's %%0%% (you can sense it on a thermometer); latent heat changes its %%1%% — and water's latent heat is enormous.
config.hint: One you read on a thermometer; the other is a change of form — ice, water, steam.

activities.anchor: water boils at 100 °C at sea level but
activities.caption: line up the refrigeration cycle
activities.name: hvacCycleOrder

config.prompt: Pressure changes boiling points — order the cycle that moves heat against its gradient:
items: Boil the fluid at low pressure indoors — it absorbs heat (the evaporator)
Compress the vapour to a hotter state — the compressor does work on it
Reject the heat outdoors as the fluid condenses (the condenser)
Expand back to low pressure to repeat (the metering device)
config.why: Boil a fluid at low pressure indoors to absorb heat, compress it to condense and reject that heat outdoors — and the heat pump is the same cycle reversed, which is why one machine can heat and cool.

activities.anchor: A quick field estimate: subtract about
activities.caption: place the dew point on the scale
activities.name: hvacDewPlace

config.prompt: Dry-bulb 25 °C, RH 50%. Using the trade's quick estimate, where is the dew point (°C)?
config.why: Subtract (100 − RH)/5 = 10 from the dry-bulb: 15 °C. Cool a pane below the dew point and you get condensation; run a cooling coil below it and you dehumidify.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the two hazards
activities.name: hvacHazardSpot

config.prompt: One line of this electrical-safety summary is wrong — click it:
lines: A thermal hazard is overheating — current flowing where it should not.
A shock hazard is current passing through a person.
It is current that harms, not voltage alone.
Around 5 milliamps through the chest is the accepted maximum harmless shock.
A higher voltage is always the more dangerous, whatever the current.
config.correction: It is current through the body that harms — very small currents matter, which is why 5 milliamps is the accepted maximum harmless shock.
config.why: Every electrical safety device addresses one of the two hazards — keep the two hazards in mind and the defences organise themselves.

activities.anchor: Modern wiring defends against both hazards with layers
activities.caption: pair each defence with its job
activities.name: hvacWiringMatch

config.prompt: The layered defences — pair each device with its job:

pairs.right: trips when current exceeds its rating — the thermal-overload backstop
held at zero volts by earthing — safe to touch even with damaged insulation
bonded to the metal case; a fault drives a large current straight to earth, tripping the breaker
compares the live current with the neutral's return; trips within milliseconds when they differ
de-energise, lock the disconnect, tag it, verify dead with a meter — capacitors hold a lethal charge after power-off

config.why: This is why the third prong on a plug must never be cut off — and why two-prong tools are the doubly insulated ones with non-conducting plastic cases.

activities.anchor: Each of the three energies punishes improvisation differently
activities.caption: file each discipline under its energy
activities.name: hvacSafetyBuckets

config.prompt: The trade's safety trio — file each discipline:

items.label: lockout/tagout: de-energise, lock, tag, verify dead
capacitors hold a lethal charge after power-off
mercaptan odourises the fuel so a leak announces itself
combustion analysis measures CO and oxygen in the flue
recovery machines and cylinders before opening any circuit
vapour displaces oxygen — an asphyxiation hazard in a confined space

config.why: High-side pressures of 1–3 MPa, regulated greenhouse gases, EPA Section 608 certification to handle refrigerant at all — each energy has its own non-negotiable discipline, and all three punish improvisation severely.

activities.anchor: the burner's job is to supply exactly enough air
activities.caption: commission the burner — choose the air
activities.name: hvacBurnerBranch

config.root: You are commissioning a gas burner. Perfect combustion of natural gas — mostly methane — unites fuel carbon with oxygen to make carbon dioxide and water vapour, releasing heat. How much air do you supply?

start.text: The analyser is connected and the flue is ready.

choices.label: Exactly enough air
choices.feedback: The carbon unites with oxygen completely — carbon dioxide, water vapour, heat released.

choices.label: Too little air
choices.feedback: The carbon stops halfway — carbon monoxide instead of carbon dioxide.

choices.label: Too much air
choices.feedback: Efficiency collapses — heat leaves up the flue in the excess.

perfect.text: The analyser reports low CO and the right oxygen and stack temperature — the numbers that say the furnace is safe and efficient.

little.text: Incomplete combustion is a tuning failure, and the analyser's carbon monoxide reading is the number that catches it.

much.text: The flue gas leaves hotter — the heat you paid for goes up the stack, and the fuel bill pays for it.

config.why: Around the chemistry sit the draft and venting systems, and the safety devices that police the flame: thermocouples and flame sensors that shut gas off if the flame fails, spill switches, and CO detectors as the household backstop.
